common_name: Whole Cloth Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal White-and-Blue-Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Whole Cloth won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 1962 and remains a benchmark amoena-pattern iris.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil; soggy conditions cause rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Whole Cloth bears pure white standards above falls washed and edged in rich blue-violet, an amoena color pattern so clean and well balanced that it earned the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 1962 and influenced decades of bicolor breeding that followed. It remains a garden-worthy heirloom for collectors wanting a piece of iris breeding history alongside modern reblooming cultivars. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center rhizome and replanting healthy outer fans about a foot apart.

Its bold, high-contrast markings still stand out in a modern iris border more than half a century after its introduction. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans about a foot apart.

Flavescens dates to 1813, making it one of the oldest tall bearded iris cultivars still passed along today, bearing soft, pale sulfur-yellow self-colored flowers on a plant that is noticeably shorter and daintier than modern hybrids bred two centuries later. Heirloom iris collectors and historic-garden restorers grow it for its documented age and its uncomplicated, old-fashioned charm rather than for flower size, since it cannot compete with modern ruffled cultivars on that front. It is exceptionally tough and easy, having survived in gardens and old homesites with essentially no care for generations. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep it vigorous.

It has been maintained in historic iris collections for over a century as an important early milestone in breeding true yellow into the tall bearded iris class. The compact, sturdy plant is exceptionally easy to grow and reliably increases into a dense clump. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans.

Its toughness and long history make it a favorite for heritage garden restorations and pass-along plant collections. It multiplies readily into a dense, weed-suppressing clump with minimal care. It has been kept in circulation for well over a century by heirloom iris collectors drawn to its historic significance and quietly pretty color blend. The plant is tough, reliable, and easy to naturalize in an old-fashioned cottage-style border. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.

It remained one of the standard garden yellows for decades after its introduction and is still grown by heirloom iris collectors today. Dusky Dancer bears deep, velvety black-purple flowers with a rich sheen that catches light differently through the day, a dramatic dark self color that pairs strikingly with pale yellow, white, or silvery companion perennials in a mixed border. Like other very dark bearded iris cultivars, the intensity of the color develops best with cool nights during bud development, so bloom can look slightly softer in an unusually warm spring. The sturdy, well-branched stalks hold flowers well above the sword-shaped foliage. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans.

Kharkov bears deep violet-blue self-colored flowers on a compact, sturdy plant that was bred and selected in Ukraine for the ability to survive winters far colder than many Western European tall bearded iris cultivars of its era could tolerate, and it has been used as breeding stock specifically for that trait. Its historic significance for cold-climate iris breeding has kept it in circulation among collectors long after flashier modern hybrids surpassed it in flower size. It is exceptionally tough and low-maintenance once established. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.

common_name: San Francisco Bearded Iris (Historic 1927 White-and-Blue Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; a 1927-era historic plicata still grown by heirloom iris collectors.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil; soggy conditions cause rhizome rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. San Francisco bears white flowers finely edged and stippled in blue-violet in the plicata pattern, a color break that was considered refined and novel when it was introduced in the late 1920s and that helped popularize plicata patterning in American iris gardens of the era. Heirloom iris collectors keep it in circulation today as an important step in the development of the plicata color class, alongside better-known later cultivars like Madame Chereau. Its plant habit is tough and easy, tolerating average garden soil with minimal fuss. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.
